transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-29
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 mins
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (CTO, Praxis), Renee Patel (ML Eng), Samir Khan (Infra)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for carving time, um this is Maya with Redwood Inference, I'm the AE on the account, with Diego from SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Jordan: Good, thanks. We're excited to hear options. Quick context: Praxis is shipping a conversational assistant embedded in our app, user-facing, sub 200ms target for token generation at 95th percentile for short replies.
[00:18] Renee: Yeah and we have some privacy constraints -- PII scrubbing, regional residency for EU, and KMS for keys.
[00:25] Maya: Got it. High level I'll run through quickstart/credits, hosted API flow, then dedicated and private alternatives; Diego can speak to perf and sizing. We'll then map to your success criteria.
[00:36] Diego: Hi all — quick note, when we say "time-to-first-token" or TTFT, we mean getting a dev to make a first successful inference from their account to a model in under an hour, ideally with example code and SDK. For production perf, there are levers — batching, prefix/KV cache, quantization, and kernel selection which matter.
[00:54] Samir: When you say "KV cache" you mean the key/value cache for autoregressive decoding? We already use a transformer-based model and worry about cold-cache spikes.
[01:02] Diego: Exactly. Automatic KV caching can keep hot prefixes in memory which lowers token latency and cost; we also do adaptive batching so interactive loads don't get crushed by large batch windows.
[01:12] Jordan: Walk me through hosted credits then — what's included in the quickstart?
[01:16] Maya: For PLG quickstart we give free credits for API usage, SDKs, example prompts, and a short pre-configured team org. Time-to-first-token — many teams get a token in minutes, but realistic end-to-end with tokenized prompts and example auth is under an hour. The credits cover both text generation and embeddings.
[01:33] Renee: Is there a limit to the model variants we can try? We want to benchmark a trimmed LLaMA variant, and possibly a larger open model.
[01:40] Diego: You can try any model in the catalog; for benchmarking we recommend pinned model versions. For Hosted we have Redwood-verified profiles so you'll see latency/cost estimates.
[01:49] Samir: Pricing — free credits are fine for devs, but for prod we need predictability. How does Dedicated compare cost-wise?
[01:55] Maya: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools. It offers predictable throughput and isolation — pricing moves to a seat/instance + usage profile vs pure per-token. Usually better for steady, high-throughput workloads; Hosted is better for getting started and bursty loads.
[02:09] Jordan: And private? We need to know about VPC and on-prem choices.
[02:13] Diego: Our Private option is customer-managed networking: private control plane, option to bring-your-own-cloud or on-prem. It includes audit logs, KMS/HSM integration, SSO, and you can pin the model artifact. There's more setup but it gives you the residency and compliance controls.
[02:28] Renee: SOC 2 reports? Certification? We need to give that to our security team.
[02:33] Maya: We have SOC 2 Type II and ISO artifacts we can share — I'll attach them. Also we can provide the Private checklist with network diagrams.
[02:41] Jordan: Cool. On perf — our 95th target is 200ms for short responses. Can Redwood reach that on Hosted?
[02:48] Diego: It depends on model size and token length. For smaller models (few hundred million to low billions) and using our streaming path with optimized kernels, hitting <200ms p95 for single-token latency is feasible regionally. For bigger models you may need Dedicated with pinned capacity or quantized variants — also consider prefix caching.
[03:10] Samir: Any rough numbers for p95 with, say, a 2B model on hosted in us-west?
[03:15] Diego: Ballpark, single-token p95 might be 120–220ms depending on load and KV warm state. With Dedicated it tightens — 80–150ms. These are rough; we should run a microbenchmark with your trace.
[03:27] Jordan: Ok that helps. On security again: what's KC? I think you said KMS/HSM earlier but the transcript from our security review misspelled a few things.
[03:36] Maya: KMS — key management service. We integrate with common KMS providers, or for Private you can use your HSM. Also SSO via SAML/SCIM and RBAC for token scoping.
[03:46] Renee: Data retention? We need retention off by default and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[03:51] Maya: Hosted has configurable retention; default is short, and we can set zero-retention for enterprise. Audit logs can be forwarded via syslog or an export connector for Private.
[04:02] Jordan: Good. Let's talk success criteria for the pilot — what should we measure?
[04:06] Diego: I'd propose: 1) functional parity on 10 canonical prompts, 2) p95 latency under X ms (we should agree target), 3) cost per 1k tokens vs baseline, and 4) a plan for go/no-go after 6 weeks.
[04:17] Jordan: Sounds reasonable. Our internal stakeholders: product owner will want cost delta, infra will validate latency, security wants SOC2 + KMS. Timeline: we'd like pilot live by mid-August.
[04:30] Maya: That's doable — we'll aim to get pricing and SOW to you within the week. For mid-August pilot start we'll need sample traffic and an infra call this week or early next to size.
[04:41] Samir: On VPC peering — with Private we prefer AWS VPC for now. Any network perf implications?
[04:47] Diego: When it's in VPC, cross-AZ latency is typical cloud LAN — very low — but you should expect network egress accounting. Private in-region gives the best latencies; Dedicated in same region also good and simpler to set up than on-prem.
[04:58] Renee: Can we do a quick POC on Hosted to validate correctness, then move to Dedicated if perf is off? We're sensitive to migration friction.
[05:05] Maya: Yes, that's a common path: PLG hosted quickstart → pilot on Hosted with credits → if steady high throughput, move to Dedicated or Private. We support canary rollouts and model pinning to keep behavior consistent.
[05:18] Jordan: Any gotchas with quantization? We want to drop to int8 for cost but worried about quality regressions.
[05:23] Diego: Quantization helps cost a lot; our Optimize team provides quantization profiles by model family. There's often small regressions—we'd recommend A/B evals on your prompt set and Redwood's quality monitoring to detect regressions. Diego: (overlap) Also some kernels are quantization-friendly and others less so.
[05:39] Renee: Who owns the evals? We want reproducible evals tied to our prompt set.
[05:44] Maya: We can help you onboard the eval set into our Optimize tooling and set regression alerts. Typically shared ownership: Praxis provides prompts and golden outputs, Redwood configures eval harness and runs baselines.
[05:55] Samir: For the pilot, what's required for infra from our side?
[06:00] Diego: For Hosted quickstart minimal: API key and dev integration, sample request trace, and a small dataset for evals. For Dedicated/Private we'll need network access details, preferred region, and compliance paperwork.
[06:11] Jordan: Ok. Let's talk pricing model — is Dedicated an annual commit?
[06:15] Maya: Dedicated is typically monthly/annual reserved capacity. We offer flexible trial reserved pools for pilots; for Private there's an enterprise license plus deployment fees. I'll include ranges in the pricing doc.
[06:26] Jordan: Any competitor differences we should watch for?
[06:29] Diego: Compared to the larger API providers, Redwood focuses on inference economics and deployment flexibility. We often get called out for better tooling around batching, KV caching, and rollout controls. But folks mention Anthropic/OpenAI for model quality and Cohere for neat embeddings.
[06:42] Renee: One more: do you support on-prem GPU boxes? We have an air-gapped requirement for a subset of workloads.
[06:48] Diego: Yes, Private on-prem deployments are supported, but they take longer — usually a multi-week project with our infra team. We also have a checklist for air-gapped installs.
[06:58] Jordan: Great. Any immediate risks you see for our timeline?
[07:02] Maya: Biggest risk is not having traffic traces and a canonical prompt set — that slows sizing. Also, legal/Security review can add time if SOC docs need legal redlining. We'll try to mitigate by sending docs early.
[07:15] Jordan: Got it. If we proceed with the Hosted pilot, how long do credits usually last?
[07:20] Maya: Credits vary — for PLG trials they're limited; for pilot we can allocate a larger credit pool tied to the SOW. We'll propose something that covers the expected token volume for 4–6 weeks of testing.
[07:31] Renee: One last technical: what's the recommended observability hook? We need token-level cost and latency per-route.
[07:37] Diego: Redwood Console exposes token-level breakdowns, per-route traces, error rates and per-model dashboards. You can also stream traces into your tracing backend via our tracing hooks.
[07:47] Jordan: Perfect. Let's surface the next steps.
[07:50] Maya: Recap: We'll send pricing + pilot SOW, SOC2/ISO artifacts, Private checklist, and Diego will send quantization/kernel guide. Praxis will share sample traffic and a prompt set. We'll schedule the tech deep-dive next week.
[08:03] Jordan: That works. Thanks all.
[08:06] Maya: Thanks, talk soon.

Post-meeting notes: the transcript above contains minor transcription artifacts; some product names spelled differently in auto-transcript (e.g., "Redwood Dedicate", "Privatey", "KV cash"). - Security: Maya to share SOC2 and KMS options; Private checklist if needed.
